blocks.content: ENTRYPOINT also defines what runs when a container starts, but unlike CMD, it is not meant to be casually overridden, it fixes the container's core behavior.
1. A Fixed Command, Not a Default One
blocks.text: 1. A Fixed Command, Not a Default One

blocks.content: Where CMD is a convenient default that anything on the command line replaces, ENTRYPOINT is treated as the container's actual purpose, arguments passed on docker run are appended to it rather than replacing it outright.

blocks.alt: ENTRYPOINT is the fixed behavior, not just a suggestion

blocks.content:
FROM python:3.11
ENTRYPOINT ["python", "app.py"]

# docker run myimage --debug
# actually runs: python app.py --debug

code.content:

# docker run myimage --debug
# actually runs: python app.py --debug

codes.dockerfile:

# docker run myimage --debug

blocks.content: The two are commonly combined: ENTRYPOINT fixes the executable, CMD supplies default arguments to it, arguments that can still be overridden without touching the fixed entrypoint itself. The full comparison is covered in the dedicated CMD vs ENTRYPOINT topic later in this module.

blocks.alt: ENTRYPOINT fixes the binary, CMD supplies default args

blocks.content: 3. Overriding It Requires an Explicit Flag
blocks.text: 3. Overriding It Requires an Explicit Flag

blocks.content: Because it is meant to be stable, replacing ENTRYPOINT entirely requires an explicit --entrypoint flag on docker run, ordinary trailing arguments are not enough, which is exactly the intended friction.

blocks.alt: A deliberate flag is required to truly replace it

blocks.content:
docker run --entrypoint bash myimage
# The only way to bypass ENTRYPOINT entirely and get a shell instead

code.content:
docker run --entrypoint bash myimage
# The only way to bypass ENTRYPOINT entirely and get a shell instead

codes.bash:
docker run --entrypoint bash myimage
# The only way to bypass ENTRYPOINT entirely and get a shell instead

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: ENTRYPOINT fixes what a container actually runs, arguments get appended to it rather than replacing it like they do with CMD.
Overriding ENTRYPOINT requires the explicit --entrypoint flag, by design, unlike CMD which anything on the command line replaces.
